title: Stability Creates Instability
concise_statement: Periods of prolonged calm encourage behaviors that eventually generate fragility and crisis.
detailed_explanation: When systems appear stable, people become more optimistic, take greater risks, use more leverage, and reduce safety margins. This accumulation of hidden fragility eventually makes the system vulnerable to shocks.
implications: Long calm periods should increase caution, not complacency.
Risk accumulates invisibly during prosperous times.
Stability can encourage excessive leverage and speculation.
Booms naturally contain the seeds of future busts.

title: Calm Plants the Seeds of Crisis
concise_statement: Perceived safety encourages behaviors that increase future vulnerability.
detailed_explanation: When people believe danger has disappeared, they reduce preparedness, ignore warnings, and optimize aggressively. This creates fragile systems highly sensitive to unexpected disruptions.
implications: Warnings are hardest to hear during stable periods.
Preparation declines when threats seem distant.

title: High Valuations Reduce Error Tolerance
concise_statement: The more optimized and expensive systems become, the less room they have for surprise or disappointment.
detailed_explanation: When expectations become excessively optimistic and assets are priced for perfection, even small negative surprises can trigger disproportionate instability.
implications: Fragility rises when systems lose slack.
Risk grows during periods of confidence.

title: Success Breeds Complacency
concise_statement: The behaviors that create success are often abandoned after success is achieved.
detailed_explanation: Discipline, caution, paranoia, and vigilance often drive early success. Once success arrives, people reduce these protective behaviors because maintaining them feels stressful or unnecessary.
implications: Long-term success requires preserving productive discipline.

title: Preparedness Declines When Risks Fade From Memory
concise_statement: As threats become historically distant, societies psychologically and structurally underprepare for them.
detailed_explanation: Humans anchor expectations to recent experience. When disasters become rare, people gradually stop allocating attention, resources, and emotional readiness toward them.

title: Good Conditions Can Generate Future Disasters
concise_statement: Positive developments can unintentionally create conditions for later negative outcomes.
detailed_explanation: Improvements and abundance often alter incentives and system structures in ways that increase future vulnerability. Excessive growth, comfort, or optimization can become destabilizing.
implications: Benefits can create hidden future costs.
Systems require balance, not maximal optimization.
Short-term success can increase long-term fragility.

title: Excess Naturally Produces Its Opposite
concise_statement: Extreme conditions tend to generate forces that reverse or counteract them.
detailed_explanation: When any condition becomes excessive—optimism, pessimism, growth, fear, stability, abundance—it often creates imbalances that eventually trigger an opposing reaction.
implications: Balance is more sustainable than maximization.
Contrarian thinking becomes valuable near extremes.

title: Human Psychology Anchors to Recent Conditions
concise_statement: People assume recent conditions are normal and project them into the future.
detailed_explanation: Humans adapt quickly to current environments and underestimate how different conditions were historically or could become again. This creates blind spots around rare but recurring risks.

title: Warnings Lose Power During Prosperity
concise_statement: The safer people feel, the less attention they pay to warnings about future danger.
detailed_explanation: When systems function smoothly for extended periods, warnings appear paranoid, unnecessary, or irrational. Success itself reduces receptiveness to cautionary signals.
implications: Preventive systems become politically vulnerable during calm periods.
Long-term preparedness is difficult to sustain socially.

title: Discovering Limits Requires Overshooting
concise_statement: Progress and adaptation often require pushing beyond perceived safe or rational boundaries.
detailed_explanation: Humans and systems frequently overshoot in both optimism and pessimism because boundaries of possibility are only discovered through experimentation beyond established limits.
implications: Cycles are partly mechanisms of discovery.
Excess is difficult to eliminate entirely.
Human systems naturally oscillate around sustainable limits.
